title: Peter and Cornelius (Acts 10)
hook: a rooftop vision tells Peter no one is unclean, and he walks into a Roman's house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananias, who was scared and went anyway, and greeted his enemy as brother Saul.

Two men, two towns on the same coast, two visions a day apart. In Caesarea, a Roman port, lives Cornelius, a centurion: an army officer. He isn't Jewish, but he honors the God of Israel, prays, and gives generously to the poor. At three in the afternoon an angel tells him: send to Joppa for Simon Peter. Next day at noon, in Joppa, Peter climbs onto a flat roof to pray while lunch is made. He's hungry. He falls into a trance: a great sheet is let down from the sky, full of every kind of animal, including ones the law of Moses says a Jew must not eat. A voice says: rise, Peter. Kill, and eat.
screen: `A ROMAN OFFICER PRAYS.` → `A HUNGRY MAN ON A ROOF.` → `RISE, PETER. KILL, AND EAT.`

segments.voice: Peter refuses: not so, Lord, I've never eaten anything common or unclean. The voice answers, in the King James Bible: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common." It happens three times. The sheet vanishes, Peter sits puzzled, and right then Cornelius's messengers are at the gate, calling for him. Today's word is Gentile, from the Latin for nations, translating the Hebrew and Greek words for the peoples of the world: anyone who isn't Jewish. Peter tells Cornelius it was not lawful for a Jew to keep company with someone of another nation, or come into his house. He goes anyway, into the officer's house, full of family and friends, and explains the vision. It wasn't about lunch: "God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean." Then: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons." God doesn't play favorites. While he's speaking, the Spirit falls on everyone listening, Gentiles included, and the believers with Peter are astonished. Christians read this chapter as the moment the church learned to welcome Gentiles as they were, without asking them to become Jewish first; many also read it as releasing Christians from the food laws. The argument wasn't over; a few chapters later, the church meets in Jerusalem to settle it. For Jews who keep them, then and now, those laws are part of their covenant with God. This story is about a door, and who's allowed through it.
screen: `WHAT GOD HATH CLEANSED.` · `GENTILE: THE NATIONS.` · `PETER WALKS IN.` · `NO RESPECTER OF PERSONS.` · then, large: `CALL NO ONE COMMON.`

segments.voice: Think of a door you don't go through: a neighbor's, a place of worship not your own, a part of town, or a conversation you keep stepping around. Picture someone calling you at the gate, as they called Peter, and ask what it would take to walk in, respectfully, as a guest; you don't have to decide today. If you pray, you can bring it to God.
Gentile. From the Latin for the nations: anyone who isn't Jewish. The day Peter walked into a Roman's house.
Your line: call no one common. Tomorrow, a knock at another door. That's day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Christians read the story of Peter and Cornelius as the moment the early church welcomed Gentiles as they were. Christian churches generally do not keep the biblical food laws, and many point to this chapter and to Acts 15 as the reason.

original.note: Greek: the nations, the peoples of the world; the root of our word ethnic. The Latin gentes gave us Gentile.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Gentile is just a non-Jew, a label.
what it means: Peter learns that God calls no one common, and walks through the door of a Roman officer's house.
what a scholar hears: Gentile is the Latin gentes for the Greek ethne and the Hebrew goyim, the nations; Acts 15 shows the church still working out what this chapter meant.
recall: Jesus taken up into God's presence

notes: Distance Caesarea to Joppa given as about thirty miles; roughly 30–35 miles. Confirm.

The script says a devout Jew 'didn't go into a Gentile's home or eat at his table' (following Acts 10:28's own statement). Practices varied in the first century; a Judaism Keeper may want softer wording.
The sentence on Jewish food laws as 'a treasured part of their covenant' is meant to prevent any supersessionist reading; confirm tone.
'Most also read it as releasing Christians from the food laws': some Christian groups keep some dietary laws (e.g., Seventh-day Adventists, Ethiopian Orthodox customs). Confirm the word 'most'.
